brief.desc: Bearish, 33/100. Gold is being repriced by an oil-driven Fed hiking cycle: the 10-year real yield rose 43bp in 20 sessions to 2.88% (FRED, Oct 1) and 2.92% on Treasury's Oct 2 curve. Even a 29k payroll miss could not hold a rally, so I am fairly confident in the direction and less sure of the speed.
brief.yr: GLD closed at 380.14 on October 2, down 0.68%, after printing a 385.22 high early and fading to a 378.11 low; December futures settled at 4,162.30, down 0.95%. September payrolls rose only 29k against an 84k consensus, cutting October hike odds from about 70% to 21.59% (CME FedWatch via FXStreet). Yields reversed higher into the close, with the 10-year real yield up 4bp to 2.92% and the 2-year up 5bp to 4.83% on Treasury's curve, and gold followed them down. DXY slipped to 101.93, so this was a rates move, not a dollar move.
brief.to: Base case (50%) is a grind lower toward about 4,050 on futures as oil stays high and a December hike stays priced; capitulation toward 3,900 (25%) if Hormuz escalation or hot data revives October hike odds; a relief rally toward 4,400 (25%) if the strait reopens and real yields fall back. The week's key events are ISM Services on October 5, FOMC minutes on October 7, jobless claims on October 8 and preliminary Michigan inflation expectations on October 9. This view flips bullish if the 10-year TIPS real yield closes below 2.60%.

brief.why: The Strait of Hormuz is the root cause. On Sep 28, Brent rebounded after Washington rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the strait; October hike odds rose to 70.3% from 64.2% and the 10-year went back above 5.2% (USAGold citing CME FedWatch), and GLD fell 3.94% that day. The Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00% on Sep 16 for the first time since 2023, and the market prices more. The pricing has a clear shape: breakevens are pinned at 2.34-2.36% while real 10s have gone from 2.45% to 2.92% in a month. Investors believe the Fed will stop the oil shock from becoming inflation, so they demand more real return, and gold has no answer to that. Friday showed how strong the regime is. A 29k payroll print with downward revisions should have broken the hiking narrative; it took October off the table but left December at 100%, and the curve finished higher. As long as oil keeps headline inflation hot, weak growth data delays hikes rather than reversing them, and gold needs a reversal. The buyers who carried gold through 2025 are not stepping in. Central-bank buying is real but slowing (23t in July, year-to-date behind 2025, WGC), a floor rather than an engine. August ETF inflows were a record (18 billion dollars, 121t, WGC), but that money came in above today's prices and is now underwater. With Managed Money still 120k net long, that leaves positions available to liquidate, not a crowded short to squeeze.
brief.cons: The loud narrative is that the October hike died, so gold bottoms here. It is half-right: October odds did collapse, but the curve and gold both sold off into Friday's close, so the market itself rejected the dovish reading. The geopolitical-haven story has the sign backwards for now, because the Hormuz shock reaches gold through oil, then the Fed, then real yields, and that channel is bearish. The crowded side is not the short: Managed Money holds 131,711 longs against 11,393 shorts (CFTC Disaggregated, Sep 29) even after a 7,071 net cut, so the bearish call is the less crowded side. What is stretched is the speed: GLD is down 7.33% in 20 sessions with real yields up 43bp, and a 20bp give-back in real yields would produce a sharp relief rally without changing the regime.
fals: Soften: the Treasury 10-year real yield closes below 2.75% on any day this week; the trend would stall and I would move toward neutral.

Invert: the 10-year TIPS real yield closes below 2.60%, the level before the Sep 23 break; that unwinds the repricing and I would flip bullish, readable daily on Treasury's curve and a day later on FRED.

Weak joint: I assume Western ETF money is now leaving, but the latest verified flows are August's record 18 billion dollar inflow; if WGC's September report, due in early October, shows holdings held up through a 7% drop, the liquidation leg of the thesis is wrong.
